en: General Principles for the *Jílüè* (Compendium) of Eminent Monks of the Imperial Ming Dynasty:
Those born during the Yuan dynasty and who passed away under the present dynasty [the Ming] are recorded; those who passed away during the Yuan are not recorded.
Regarding the ten masters beginning with Chushi, each has their own *yùlù* (recorded sayings); it is impossible to include the complete texts of all of them. As for the preceding...
The public sermons given by the Master while presiding over the hall, his verses on *niansong* (eulogies) and *tiyong* (inscriptions), and other miscellaneous writings have all been recorded in part.
As for the appended materials, these include the prefaces and funerary inscriptions for various virtuous teachers found within the collected works of the Song Dynasty scholar Xu Jinglian;
of these, only those who were also associated with our own dynasty have been recorded in part.
Furthermore, as for the appended [entries]: because the eras of the masters Puzhi,
Chushi Qi, Dufeng Shan, and Konggu Long were lost from the records, their names have been added to the catalog.
Chan Master Tianqi Rui, Chan Master Jiefeng Ying, Chan Master Chushan Qi,
Chan Master Xingyuan Ming, Chan Master Xueting, Chan Master Xiaoyan Bao,
and Chan Master Guyin Qin.
Appendix:
Inscriptions on Ancient Tripods by Chan Master Xuechuang Guang, Chan Master Nantang Yu,
Chan Master Jingshan Yuekong, Chan Master Foguang Puzhao, and Chan Master Bifeng Jin.
Dongming Master Ri and Gufeng Master De also appended [their records] following those of Goryeo Master Pujie.
A Compendium of Eminent Monks of the Imperial Ming Dynasty,
compiled by the Bhikṣu Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple, Ming Dynasty;
including Chan Master Chushi Qi.
The Master’s actual name was Fan Qi; Chu Shi was his pen-name. He was a native of Xiangshan County in Ningbo Prefecture and belonged to the Zhu clan.

At the age of nine, he received instruction in the Confucian classics from Master Mo (Nuweng). At sixteen, he shaved his head and donned the monastic robes. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained a profound realization. Thereafter—
When Master Yuansou Duan entered the capital, he heard the sound of the drums at the Western Tower, and his sweat fell like rain.

He then composed a verse: "I have caught a single speck of snow in a red furnace; it is, in truth, the ice of the Yellow River in the sixth month. Upon meeting Yuansou, Yuansou gave him his approval. At that time, Baoen Monastery was vacant and awaited him;
the Master reluctantly accepted the invitation and built a residence in the western hall, intending to spend the remainder of his life there. Thus did the Master [establish himself].
His physical stature was short and small, yet his spiritual countenance was refined and lucid. He upheld and propagated the True Dharma with a sense of shamelessness and sublime joy.
His worldly lifespan was seventy-five years, and his monastic seniority was sixty-three years. Six volumes of his recorded sayings are currently in circulation.

Ascending the hall for the New Year’s Eve small *chan* session: "Excellent! The board has struck three times; all you who possess true knowledge have come to attend. Since you already well know the proper season, I shall not speak further.
O worthy ones, once spoken, it is not spoken again; now it has been spoken twice. Once heard, it is not heard again..."
No longer heard. Now it has been heard again. Clear in every head; realized in every object. In accordance with principle and in accordance with phenomena, spanning from antiquity to the present.
It is not the mind of Nirvana, nor is it the True Dharma Eye. Such and such—throughout the three periods of time, all Buddhas have only said that one knows for oneself.
Not such and not such—throughout the six generations of Patriarchs, there was no place to open their mouths. Even if...
Even if one were to attain realization before words are spoken, it would still be a lingering within the shell and a delusion of confinement.

Even if one were thoroughly proficient in the meaning beneath a single phrase, one could not avoid being touched by deluded and frantic views. Now, upon the red furnace, a single point of snow is gathered; upon the withered tree, a few specks of blossoms are scattered.
For you all, I mark this particular occasion: the dying lamp follows the end of winter; the bursting firecrackers usher in the spring. Again, he raised his alms bowl.
Mount Yun said, "The path that goes upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages. Ciming said, "The path that goes upward is not so even for the thousand sages.
Miaoxi said, "The path that goes upward is like the sound of a hot bowl ringing. The Master said, "These three great elders have exhausted their powers to the utmost."
"You have only succeeded in clarifying the path leading downward. As for the path leading upward, you will not have even dreamed of it for as long as a donkey lives.

In a general discourse delivered while ascending the hall, [the Master] raised this case: A monk asked Qianfeng, "The *Bhagavāns* of the ten directions all share the single path to the gate of Nirvana. I wonder, what is this path?"
"Where is the head? Feng drew a line with his staff and said, "It is right here. The Master said, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds.
The monk recounted the previous conversation and asked Yunmen about it. Yunmen said, "The fan leaps up to the thirty-third heaven."
"It hits right on the nose of Śakra. A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow of the staff; the rain pours down like an overturned basin.
The Master said, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds. Suddenly, if someone were to come forth and ask, "Does such a critique by Tianning satisfy the intent of those two great elders?
I would say to him, "Ten thousand miles of white clouds. Hehehe! Ralari! Ralari! Ra!
"Ra li! Across every land and in every speck of dust, who can know how many? The 'Stone Capable of Courage' at the crossroads suddenly sucks dry the waters of the vast ocean.
You fellows, you eggplants and gourds—how could you possibly know this? He struck the meditation seat and rose.
That evening, during the informal discourse (*xiaochan*), a monk asked: "The Buddhas do not appear in the world; the Patriarchs did not come from the West.

The Buddha-dharma pervades the world, yet those who discuss the profound do not open their mouths. Since the Buddha-dharma pervades the world, why do they not open their mouths to discuss the profound?
The Master said: "The Southern Dipper has seven stars; the Northern Dipper has eight. The monk pressed further: "I do not understand the principle of this. How is it so? The Master said: "Go."

"The road to the Western Heaven is far, extending over one hundred thousand *li*. It is said: 'To vigorously promote this matter before the assembly of devas and humans, one must be a monk of genuine caliber;
if one is not a monk of genuine caliber, one cannot avoid being ridiculed by others.'"
Just as that Zen practitioner posed a question a moment ago, you answered him in such a way that he could not grasp it.
Let me repeat it once more: "Since the Buddha-dharma pervades the world, why does your mouth remain closed when speaking of the profound?
Before the sound of the eaves has ceased from last night’s rain, the lightning streaks are already linked to the thunder of the night to come."
A small *canshan* (summer retreat) discourse. A monk asked, "What is Chan in the mountains? The Master said, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind its head.
The monk pressed further, "What is Chan in the city? The Master said, "A single brick on a crossroads. The monk pressed again.
"What is Zen in the village? The Master said, "A person from Fusang plants fields in Shensi.
The student replied, "Thank you for answering my question. The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! Then he continued: "Food and clothing sustain life; one day cannot be without them.

A broom and rag robe withstand cold and heat; coarse food cures the withering of the body. Yesterday was the third spring month; today is the ninth summer month. Why do you not take advantage [of this time]?"
While the physical body is strong and healthy, one brushes aside the teachings and the path of birth and death becomes clear. If you wish to go, you go; if you wish to stay, you stay.
Who can obstruct you? Who can hinder you? Is this not magnificent? Is this not joyful?
But tell me, how do you brush aside the path of birth and death? Empty-handed, holding a hoe; walking, riding a water buffalo. A person passes over a bridge...
People pass over the bridge; the water flows, yet the bridge does not flow. If you do not understand, I shall provide you with a commentary:
Empty-handed, one grasps a hoe; A galloping horse mounts a high tower. Walking, one rides a water buffalo; In the midst of clamor, one is cold and desolate.
People pass over the bridge; The rice basket remains hungry. The bridge flows, yet the water does not flow; One stirs the fire to seek floating bubbles. Time does not wait for man.
"San. He then cited the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Do not suppress or extinguish the various deluded minds.
Abide within the realm of deluded thoughts without applying analytical knowledge; in this absence of analytical knowledge, do not discriminate as to what is real. The Master said:
"If that is so, one may say 'it exists,' and one may also say 'it does not exist. One may go upward, and one may also go downward. It is attained."
"It can be attained; it cannot be attained, yet it can also be attained. A few wisps of white clouds enshroud an ancient temple; a single ribbon of green water winds around a verdant mountain.

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Once one becomes a village abbot, it will be difficult to emerge for ten thousand kalpas. Truly a great difficulty, a great difficulty! If you are such a man," he said.

The words of the Buddhas and the words of the Patriarchs do not remain stored within one's breast; they leap forth toward other worlds. How much more so regarding the shallow and mundane studies of this world?
Even if one can recite the four Vedas, it only increases delusive thoughts—what can such things accomplish?
One merely consumes the saliva and spittle of others, with no end in sight. It is better to be without affairs. When you see me say "without affairs," do not simply take it to mean being idle.
Furthermore, events and circumstances can be contested; however, if you wish to truly reach the state of non-action, you must apply yourself with desperate effort.

Only by undergoing a "great death" and finding life within that death can you transcend Vairocana and surpass Śākyamuni, moving freely through a hundred layers and a thousand folds, penetrating in all directions.
The patriarchal nostrils and the supreme vehicle of the lineage have all been swept away; there is no need to bring them forth. Yunmen said:
"Today I am entangling you with weeds: dung-ash, dung-fire, mired pigs and scabby dogs who do not recognize good from evil, making their living in a pit of excrement.
If you can leap out of this dung pit, then come to my hands and receive a blow of the staff."
Addressing the assembly: Look at such a time as this! Brothers who are determined to study the Way, where would you put your packs?

For what purpose have those who came before established this lineage and its teachings? It is certainly not merely for the sake of a few local relatives or Dharma kin, nor to provide for one’s own belly.

Reigning in ignorance, they form swarms and bands to create the karma of hell. They push the Buddha-dharma and the path of meditation to one side, yet how could they know that karmic retribution is ultimately unavoidable?
There, amidst the mountains of blades and trees of swords, the boiling cauldrons and glowing embers, no one can take their place.

Today, throughout the great monasteries and forest retreats, from north to south and east to west, there is not one in ten thousand who has survived since the outbreak of the military upheaval. Because of this...

Why is this so? It is because your evil deeds have reached their full measure and the fruits of your karma have ripened; you must experience for yourself what you have done—whom else could you possibly make bear the burden?
When the Patriarch urged you to leave the household life, it was certainly not merely for the sake of food, clothing, fame, or profit, nor to abandon your hometown and leave your wellspring behind.
It is solely because the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift. One must seek out teachers and visit friends, earnestly investigating until clarity is reached.
Then, with a sudden burst, one shall become a Buddha or a Patriarch; one shall repay the profound kindness of one's parents; one shall deliver all people in the world.
If it were not for this, why would one leave the household life? Reflecting coolly upon it, the ancient style is truly excellent: when hungry, one begs for food; when cold...
He mends his robes, takes a single meal at midday, and dwells for one night beneath a tree. Lodging as a traveler through the three realms, he demonstrates the coming and going of a single cycle;
only when ignorance is forever severed does one truly achieve the Buddha-way. Have you not seen National Teacher Wuye address the assembly, saying:
"After the ancients had attained their realization, they lived in thatched huts and stone chambers, eating rice cooked in a broken-legged cauldron for twenty or thirty years. This is called..."
He did not harbor profit in his heart nor take thought for wealth and treasures. Forgetting the affairs of the human world, he concealed his traces among the mountain crags and thickets.
Though kings commanded him to come and feudal lords invited him to attend, he neither came nor responded.

How could he be compared to those like us who crave fame and love gain, wallowing in the ways of the world like petty peddlers who forget the great fruit in their pursuit of minor desires? To point it out in this way is truly most discerning.
It is clear: cultivating merit is not as good as avoiding transgressions; much emptiness is not as good as a little reality.

Within this circle of light beneath the seam of the robe, who is without their share? Do not let it be lost; you must grasp it directly, and then you shall stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you say my words are false, I am willing to enter the Hell of the Plucked Tongue.

Addressing the assembly: In the teachings there are six recollections—recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of the precepts, recollection of the heavens, and recollection of giving.

But what does one recollect under the gate of the patched-robed monks? If you say it is the recollection of the Buddha, then by reciting the word "Buddha," you would have to rinse your mouth for three days;

this cannot be the recollection of the Buddha. If you say it is the recollection of the Dharma, it is said that even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma; this cannot be it either.
To contemplate the Dharma: the pure practitioner does not enter nirvana, and the precept-breaking bhikṣu does not enter hell;
this is contemplating the Saṃgha. Upholding or violating precepts merely binds the body; since there is no body, there is nothing to bind; this is contemplating the Śīla.
There is no peace in the three realms, which are like a burning house; this is contemplating the Deva. Both giver and receiver...
Regarding the object given, the three wheels are empty and quiescent; all are ungraspable. One must not harbor the thought that "this is giving.
Is it then non-thought? The moment there is non-thought, it is already thought. To avoid drowning only to leap into fire—your illness becomes even more profound.

Even if you were to be uniquely liberated and without dependence, you would still not yet be fit to be a servant to this mountain monk. Do you wish to understand? For a thousand years, there has been no shadow.
[The story of] the tree. Nowadays, there are bottomless boots.
Once Yunmen held up his staff and said: "Ordinary people truly say it exists; those of the Two Vehicles analyze it and say it does not exist;
Pratyekabuddhas call it illusory existence; Bodhisattvas realize its very substance is emptiness. When a patch-robed monk sees this staff, he simply calls it—"
He makes a staff. When walking, he simply walks; when sitting, he simply sits; in all cases, one must not move it.

Miaoxi said, "I am not like the old man Yunmen, who carves a hollow in empty space. He suddenly picked up the staff and said, "This staff does not belong to existence, nor does it belong to non-existence;
it does not belong to illusory existence, nor does it belong to immediate emptiness. He struck the ground once and said, "Ordinary people and those of the two vehicles..."
Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas all turn toward this very place, each according to their own capacity, fully making use of it.
Yet, within the sphere of the monk, it acts as a source of harm and enmity: when one wishes to walk, one cannot walk; when one wishes to sit, one cannot sit.
To take a single step forward, one is bewildered by the staff and loses the way; to take a single step back, one has one's nostrils pierced by the staff. It is simply this.
Is there anyone here now who does not have a taste for this? Come forth and meet with this staff! If there is none, next year there will be new branches;
the spring wind’s vexation shall never cease. Ordinary people should not give rise to the view of existence;

those of the Two Vehicles should not give rise to the view of non-existence; Pratyekabuddhas should not give rise to the view of illusory existence; and Bodhisattvas should not give rise to the view of [inherent] reality.
The essence is precisely the view of emptiness; one must not let this pass.

This old fellow Yunmen was so preoccupied with gazing at white waves that he lost his oar, causing all the patch-robed monks under heaven to fall into the trap of the staff. This cannot be overlooked; it would be best to bury him whole in a single pit.
To cite an ancient precedent: there was once an old woman who offered her wealth and invited Master Zhaozhou to recite the Great Canon (Tripitaka).

Zhaozhou descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated it once, and said, "The recitation of the Canon is finished. When the people returned to inform the old woman, she said, "I came specifically to request the recitation of one entire Canon;
why has the Master only recited half? Miaoxi remarked, "Among the assembly, some have discussed this, saying..."
What is that "half-treasury"? Some say it is to circumambulate once more; some say it is to snap one's fingers; some say it is to cough once;
some say it is to give a shout; some say it is to clap once. Such a view is simply a lack of shame.

If it were truly that half-treasury, let alone Zhaozhou circumambulating once more—even if one were to circumambulate hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, or billions of times—it would still not suffice.

Within the portion belonging to the old woman, one can only obtain half of the *piṭaka*. Even if one were to circumambulate Mount Sumeru hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times, within the portion belonging to the old woman, one would still only obtain half of the *piṭaka*.

Even if all the old *ho-shangs* in the world were likewise to circumambulate it hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of times, within the portion belonging to the old woman, they too would only obtain half of the *piṭaka*. Even if the mountains and rivers...
The great earth, the myriad phenomena of the universe—whether grasses or trees—all possess the mark of the broad and long tongue.
With one voice and many mouths, from this day until the end of the future, even regarding the old woman’s portion, they can only attain half of the Tripiṭaka.
Do you all wish to recognize the old woman? After a long silence, he said: "The embroidered mandarin ducks are displayed for you to behold; I do not hold back the golden needle."
Duzhenren’s teacher said: "This old woman claimed that Zhaozhou had only turned half of the *Tripiṭaka*; she was merely playing with a false image as if it were real.
At that time, he should have simply said: 'Why do you not realize it before you have even circumambulated the meditation seat?'"
Deshan raised the topic for a small-scale assembly, saying: "Tonight, this old monk will not answer questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows.
At that time, a monk came forward and bowed; Deshan struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question;
why did you strike me? Deshan asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "From Silla. Deshan said, "Not yet..."
"Stepping over the gunwale—well-deserving of thirty blows. Fayan said, "The Great and Small Deshan have split their discourse into two pieces.
Yuanming said, "The Great and Small Deshan have the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake. Xuedou said, "Deshan wielded the sovereign authority beyond the pass;
he possessed the sword that, if one does not cut when it is appropriate to cut, will invite chaos. If you wish to recognize the Korean monk, he was merely a headbanger."
A blind man clinging to a pillar;

before the poison-drum has even been struck, the ducks have already heard the thunder. Before the net that covers the heavens has been drawn in, the leaping scales have already surged through the waves.
Old Deshan! Old Deshan! When the true command is put into action, it is no mere matter of casualness. Fayen added his own arrow to this.
Pointing upward to the peak, the perfect clarity further sweeps away [delusions] before the sound. The Master Xuedou’s fragrance flows through the ages;
with a long sword in hand, he personally wields it.
He cites how Deshan, carrying his staff, arrived at Guishan; he ascended the Dharma hall, passing from east to west, and from west to east.

Guishan sat in silence, paying him no heed. Deshan said, "Nothing, nothing," and went down. He spoke again, "Nor should you be so hasty. Thereupon, he assumed the full ceremonial demeanor and went to see Guishan.
Holding up his sitting mat, he said, "Preceptor! Guishan reached for his whisk, whereupon Deshan let out a shout.

At that moment, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall, put on his straw sandals, and departed. That evening, Guishan asked [his attendant]: (Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "Guishan asked" at the end of the evening inquiry. A complete translation would require the subsequent dialogue.)
The Head Seat asked, "Where was the newly arrived monk just now? The Head Seat replied, "At that time, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went off wearing his straw sandals.
Guishan said, "Do you recognize this fellow? In the future, he will perch upon the summit of a solitary peak, build a grass hut, and go about reviling the Buddhas and scolding the Patriarchs."
The two masters met; there was neither back nor face. Their eyes were like shooting stars, their spiritual mechanisms like flashes of lightning.

As he raised his sitting cloth, he briefly revealed his sharp edge; as he reached for the whisk, he momentarily seized the moment of swift opportunity. Hereafter, he will build a thatched hut on a solitary peak:
the ox-head points north, the horse-head points south.

Since you have been designated as an Elder (sthavira) and have emerged into the world to act as a human guide, it is like using a golden surgical probe to scrape away the film from one's eyes; this is no small matter.

If you should injure the blade or commit an error of hand, you will not escape the piercing of your own eye. How perilous and dangerous! There is no room for even a hair’s breadth of negligence; how could you allow yourself to remain in blind ignorance?
A bag. Dropping his three-inch tongue, he deceives people with empty talk. Look at him: when he first arrived at Jingkou Temple, he already had some flashes of insight;
yet when it came to the point of letting go, there was still leakage. Later, he went to Huating to see the Boatman.
When the Boatman said to him, "Three inches from the hook—why do you not speak? he could not say a word. The Boatman struck him across the mouth with a single stroke of the oar. The pole.
The strands of hair on your head are for you to handle; do not disturb the clear waves, for your intent will naturally be extraordinary.
At this, he attained great enlightenment. Therefore it is said: "To practice Chan, one must first attain awakening; having awakened, one must then meet a true person.
If you do not meet such a person, you will merely become a fabricating Chan practitioner, preaching a blind and ignorant Chan that ruins people's children wherever you go. This is the foremost point.
One’s fundamental capacity must be upright; one's practice must be clear and lucid. Whether the monastery grounds are large or small, leave such matters outside the scope of concern.
Under Linji, Fengxue, and Shoushan, how often did they gather three hundred or five hundred followers? Yet to this day, their Way has spread throughout the world.
As the saying goes: "The mountain does not need to be high; it becomes famous because there is an immortal upon it."
Furthermore, it is said that as soon as these "brothers" open their mouths, they declare, "I am a Chan practitioner.
Yet when asked what Chan is, they merely glance here and there, their mouths hanging like a flat pole. How bitter! How unjust!

Having partaken of the food of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, they do not go about attending to their fundamental task, but instead prattle on with worldly phrases and literary texts, shouting at the top of their lungs without the slightest sense of restraint.
This is utterly shameless. There are those who do not seek to investigate and clarify their original face prior to the birth of their parents upon the meditation cushion;
instead, they coldly imitate the "guest pounding rice," hoping thereby to seek blessings and expiate karmic obstacles. This is far removed from the Way.
To concentrate the mind and collect the thoughts, withdrawing all phenomena back into emptiness: as soon as a thought arises, one must immediately suppress it. It is like...
This kind of view is that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism—a dead person whose soul will not return.

Furthermore, there are those who falsely identify with the capacity to feel anger, the capacity to feel joy, the capacity to see, and the capacity to hear; they believe that once these are clearly recognized, the task of a lifetime of study is finished.
Let me ask you this: when impermanence arrives and you are burned into a pile of ashes, what about this capacity to feel anger and joy?
Where does that which is able to see and hear go? To practice Chan in such a manner is like "quicksilver-silver" Chan;

this silver is not real—it flows away as soon as it is smelted. Because I asked you, "What do you usually take as your object of inquiry? you replied, "I am instructed to contemplate 'the myriad dharmas return to one.
When I asked, "Where does that 'one' return? you again told me only to understand it in this way. Today, for the first time, I have come to know [the truth].
"No. It is simply that you have requested a *huatou*. I say there is nothing wrong with the ancient *gong'an*.
Your eyes are fundamentally correct; it is because of your teacher that they have become distorted. Although he was urged repeatedly, [Wuzu] would not yield.
*Pure Land Verses (A Brief Selection of Ten)* There is an Amitābha within one’s own mind;
The moment a single thought arises, it is separated by a thousand peaks. Within this, why wait for the light to reflect back? Directly, it turns into seeking outward.
Green waters and blue mountains are all the wondrous body; Yellow orioles and purple swallows are all... *(Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)*
Mysterious Sound: Ordinary beings, because their greed and anger are so heavy, Do not realize their bodies dwell within a forest of jewel-trees.
Far off they point toward their hometown at the edge of the setting sun; The single path of return is as straight as a bowstring.

In the sky, melodies play every kind of music; Upon the water, flowers bloom in clusters of lotuses. The branches and trunks of various trees become a hundred jewels; Their communal dwelling and sustenance surpass [all else].
O Devas, may my Master grant his grace and accept me; let not fifty years of diligent devotion be in vain. One lotus bud contains one holy embryo;
when a lifetime’s merit is perfected, a flower blooms. Necklaces of jewels appear according to his will;
vessels brimming with *sudhā* arrive with every thought. The golden hall emits a light that swallows sun and moon; the jade towers have no space to contain it.
Dust and grime [are cleared away]. The Dharma King has discoursed for me on the ultimate truth; it truly makes the void smile until its cheeks are full.
About to enter the Dharma assembly to pay homage to the Golden Immortal, I gradually follow the fragrant breeze out from the precious lotus.

The light from the red *uṣṇīṣa* flows on inexhaustibly; the golden-purple body’s marks shine boundlessly. Layer upon layer, the jeweled nets hang down to the level ground; each and every flower pedestal connects [to the next].
The distant heavens; rare events within the realms of all Buddhas—clearly manifest before me like images in a bright mirror.
An inch of time is an inch of gold; I urge you to recite the Buddha’s name and quickly turn your heart back [to the Dharma].

Even if one dwells in the noble halls of the Phoenix Terrace and Dragon Palace, one cannot avoid the encroachment of wrinkled skin and white hair. Before the incense smoke within the cauldron has even dispersed, the celestial carriage in the void has already departed.
Gazing afar, though every speck of dust and every world-system is pure, only the Vow-power of Amitābha is profound.
Towers of gold and terraces of jade; a ground of lapis lazuli, free from even a trace of dust. The Land of Purity is but one’s own mind, without high or low;
the Self-nature Amitābha neither departs nor arrives. The crimson sun has never truly set beyond the heavens; the white lotus exists only within the mind.
Rooted and planted: when the obstacles of sentient beings are heavy, one must maintain visualization. When visualization reaches its limit and emotion vanishes, the eyes open wide.
Do not compare the womb-prison to a lotus pond; quickly claim a branch within that pool. Seated upon the precious flower, you become a child of the Buddha;
why trouble the compassionate mother to bathe an infant? With the mouth feasting on the true delicacies of Dharma-joy, the mind attains the wondrous gate of illumination.
In general, on the day Master Zongti returned from his meditative retreat before the Prajñā Terrace, he caused people to long remember the Master of Yanmen.
He spoke much of seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss to the west; yet in the end, it is not separate from the pure mind. Empty reflections entering the pond are all emerald green;
sunlight piercing through the trees is entirely golden. Though such phenomena are like dreams and illusions and are not real, when the principle is reached, it is perfect and eternal.
Profound indeed! The eighty-four thousand marks and signs of physical excellence—please sit upright and strike the depths of the numinous breast.
How can the praises of the country of Sumati ever be exhausted? It is not the same as the Buddha-realms of other directions. A hundred flavors, both sour and sweet, forever fill the bowl;

the body is light and vigorous, able to roam at will through space. At the very first thought, one attains the patience of non-arising; even those bound by all fetters can be taught to dwell in the past.
The Transmission of Life: Records of Rebirth Past and Present. Throughout the realms as numerous as dust motes, the breeze of compassion fans;

When the mind opens through the height of mindfulness and one beholds the Buddha, One naturally arrives at the emerald lotus pond. After thousands upon thousands of kalpas, the fires of hell’s retribution are purified;
The light of the jade trees branches out in tens of millions of limbs. One never tires of deep conversation with virtuous friends; The wondrous speech of the numinous birds is truly [sublime].

Drifting and sinking; the dust of worldly toil rolls on like mountains piled high. The karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, as deep as the ocean.

It is understood. If one is a practitioner of the Way who is truly of the original substance, they shall take the entire dharma-realm of the ten directions as their hall for the period of Perfect Enlightenment.

Now, those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name should know that the Buddha is precisely the mind. Yet, one must examine what this mind is.
One must observe from where this single thought of reciting the Buddha’s name arises; furthermore, one must see through and realize who it is that is observing.
Herein lies the point of entry, by which one will understand the meaning of Chan Master Yuanwu’s words: "It is not the mind, it is not..."
The Buddha is not a thing; what, then, is he? Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space;
it manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When one realizes empty space, there is neither 'is' nor 'is-not'.

What is called "mind" here is not the mind of discursive thought or conceptual deliberation, but rather the mind that is empty, luminous, perfectly still, vast, and signless. It is the [nature] of all Buddhas of the three periods of time...
That which is realized is this very mind. That which the sentient beings of the six realms are ignorant of is this very mind.
The Buddhas realize it through awakening and thus it is called *bodhi* (enlightenment); sentient beings are deluded by it and thus it is called *kleśa* (affliction).

It does not increase in the sages, nor does it decrease in the ordinary; one does not possess it upon attaining it, nor is it non-existent upon losing it. When deluded, it is the condition for karma; when awakened, it is named Buddha.

As for its nature: one should know that delusion and awakening reside within oneself; gain and loss do not come from another. One must realize that this mind, from kalpas past until now, has fundamentally been without birth or extinction, and originally neither defiled nor pure.
Its solitary radiance is bright and clear; its entire substance is without dependence. Its wondrous function is true and eternal, pervading the entirety of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*.
It has no form or shape that can be seen, and no sound or resonance that can be heard. Although it is without marks, it is not the case that there are no marks.
The Thesis: Although it is said that there is no sound, the absence of sound is not non-responsive; it is the root of all forms and appearances, and the valley for all sounds and echoes.
Form and emptiness are non-dual; movement and stillness are as one. Every phenomenon is empty and harmonious; every particle is liberated. Thus we know: when the mind exists, phenomena exist;
when the mind is empty, phenomena are empty. When the mind is deviant, everything is deviant; when the mind is correct, [everything is correct].

All is correct. If one thoroughly understands this mind, then phenomena (*dharma*) do not exist either. Since both mind and phenomena are non-existent, then all names, signs, right, and wrong are empty.

When names, signs, right, and wrong are empty, then the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as form and emptiness, light and darkness, are immediately and directly fused with the person’s own nature, the Buddha-mind, in its very essence; there is no longer any separation or obstruction. Regarding this, layman:
If one is able to believe and enter [this state], then there is no further distinction between what has been realized and attained by the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity.
Furthermore, what need is there to discuss the categories of ordinary person versus sage, delusion versus enlightenment, gain versus loss?

Even if this is not yet the case, there is no need to separately seek the mysterious and the subtle, nor to loathe clamor and grasp at stillness; simply sweep away and clear out all the intellectual views and insights accumulated during your daily life. Solely...
Simply lift up the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" and place it within your breast; investigate it silently and in stillness. Constantly rouse the spirit of doubt, asking:
"Who, ultimately, is this one who recites the Buddha's name? Examine and investigate this repeatedly.

You must not engage in speculative reasoning regarding existence or non-existence, nor should you harbor a mind waiting for enlightenment. If even a speck of delusive thought remains in the mind, it will all [obstruct realization].
These are obstacles. You must simply strike them down until the chest is empty and vast, devoid of even a single thing.
Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, and even in places of stillness or clamor, leisure or busyness, do not employ any discrimination or calculation.

You need only maintain the continuity of thought-moments, with mind after mind without interruption. When this practice becomes pure and unified over time, it will naturally become tranquil and light.

When you are at ease, meditative concentration will naturally manifest before you. Should your right mindfulness fail to remain singular and pure, and if dullness or distraction should arise, do not attempt to suppress them with the mind.
Instead, simply let go of the *huatou* (critical phrase) lightly and turn the light back upon yourself to reflect:
look from where these delusive thoughts and dullness arise. By this single act of reflection, the delusive thoughts and dullness will, in that very moment, vanish of their own accord.
Thus, [the mind] suddenly comes to rest. If one maintains this mindfulness with steadfast persistence over a long period, there will indeed be no regression or loss.

Suddenly, as the practice enters the subtle and wondrous state, one realizes neither consciously nor unconsciously that the mass of doubt has been crushed to pieces in a single squeeze. The defilements of kalpas melt away and disintegrate in that very moment;

He passed away in the nineteenth year of the Hongwu era at the age of sixty-nine, with fifty-eight years of monastic seniority.

This monk failed to grasp the opportunity when it arose; he missed Yunmen’s meaning, and until this very day, it has blocked the streets and filled the alleys with no place to rest.

A lively idler! Furthermore, he pressed Yunmen so hard that Yunmen was at a loss for what to do; when he let go, he could not gather it back, and when he gathered it, he could not let it go.
Is this not the mark of a true man? Even though Huanji acted in such a way, he too must have exerted no small amount of effort.
But tell me, is there still a place where one can find rest? Speaking on his behalf, [Huanji] said: "Look at what Yunmen says. The ancient pond is clear.
The stewards and others—each of you is a single fragment of true radiance from throughout vast kalpas, yet it has been buried within the vast expanse of karmic consciousness.

Amidst the arising and ceasing of thoughts, you find yourselves in a deep pit of darkness; if you wish to seek deliverance, know that this matter is like a person scaling a precipice ten thousand fathoms high:
one must be able to let go personally before success can be achieved. Furthermore, have you not heard it said: "It is not until one has passed through a single freezing coldness..."?
"Bone! How could one possibly capture the fragrant scent of the plum blossom?

If it were otherwise, one would further weary oneself by casting this illusory guest into the white lotus pond—pure as ice and smooth as jade—only to drag through the mud and water and plant the seeds of karma. Thus it is for now and for the future.
At all times, remain as bare and empty as a pauper. Look nakedly at that which existed before your parents were born;
this is your original face. *Hūṃ*. Exhausting this present moment of thought from beginning to end, you must strive to reach a clear and distinct understanding.

At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and received the full precepts, subsequently attending Master Huangmei. His diligence was excessive, causing him to stagnate in a state of profound stillness.

Thereupon, I realized the meaning of the phrase "a field manifesting upon a hair-tip," and for the first time understood that our dwelling between heaven and earth is illusory, like a dream or a journey.
Another year later, while composing a verse on the yellow oriole, I suddenly encountered a master who said of this line: [The text ends here.]
Not yet having grasped the Dharma, my mind remained outside the meaning beyond words; through this, my mental obstructions were suddenly dispelled. Speaking spontaneously, I said:
"With deep feeling, I trust myself to cherish the spring light; it flies into the gardens, that realm of brocade and embroidery. I remember how it startled me from my dream at the small window."
"Red apricot blossoms fill the courtyard, bearing the slanting sun. He then composed a regulated poem on "Mountain Dwelling" in the style of Yongming.
On the eve of the New Year in the Wushen year of the Hongzhi era, he suddenly heard the sound of a bell; his practice over several years became vividly manifest at that moment.

Spontaneously he said: "The resonance is perfect, yet the mind does not hear; The great thousandfold world is illuminated as one. Having brushed past the ultimate barrier, No further mystery or subtlety remains. [Seal] Yi-mao. Rest.
Master Xiū was invited by the Jing Temple in Hunan, and I again attached myself to him, inquiring and investigating day after day until I finally received his seal of approval (*inka*).

Now, illusion (*māyā*) is the trace of the provisional, and the provisional is the mark of illusion. When illusion arises, the provisional perishes; when the provisional is fully realized, it is entirely illusion.

As illusion pursues the provisional, the provisional is entirely illusion. It is like flowers appearing to a cataract-afflicted eye—the mountains, rivers, and great earth; yet when the cataract-flowers do not arise, all is empty space.
The ultimate reality is the locus of illusion; truly, it is like a child’s play.
Thus was the instruction given by Master Guyin Qin.
Even if one encounters an opening instruction, it is difficult to awaken to it all at once. One must rely on a *huatou* (critical phrase) to force open the heart-mind.
Through long-term practice, day after day, ground and refine it a thousand times, like a hen brooding her eggs, steaming them with constant warmth. Suddenly, one day, when the proper time arrives—
Or, when encountering the triggering of causes and conditions, the mind and eyes may finally attain awakening. As the ancients said: "Each flower has its own season for blooming;
the spring orchid and the autumn chrysanthemum do not share the same path. In performing spiritual practice, one should leave behind clamor and cut off all external entanglements.

Stilling all distracting thoughts, single-mindedly maintain the original koan. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether encountering suffering or joy, adversity or favor—at all times, do not allow it to be forgotten.
Keep it present at every moment, focusing the mind and aligning the intention with earnest and persistent reflection.
Moment by moment, investigate for yourself: turn back and look at this very person who is able to pursue and question—what kind of person is this?

If you can cast your doubt in this way, doubting again and again until you reach the point where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves, where the tree falls and the vines wither, where there is no room for deliberation, and where mind and object are forgotten—suddenly the mass of doubt will burst apart, and the flowers of the mind will bloom.
It bursts forth clearly; great awakening manifests before one, and one suddenly perceives one's own original Buddha-nature. This singular radiance is not obtained from without.
If you truly attain such a perspective, you must still seek out a master of high realization to resolve what is heterodox and what is orthodox;
you must not rest content with this alone. Only then can it be called "entering the gate" and only then "attaining the ground."

Whatever good or evil one perceives while sitting arises entirely from failing to maintain observation during the practice, engaging in improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), and merely closing the eyes to sit in stillness with a lack of mental vigor.
When the mind follows the flow of sensory objects, half-dreaming and half-awake, one may become attached to the pleasure of stillness, thereby perceiving various visionary states.
For one who practices with the correct cause, when it is time to sleep, they should simply sleep.
Upon a single awakening and a single alertness, immediately rouse your spirit, rub your eyes, clench your teeth, and tighten your fists.
Look directly at where the *huatou* (critical phrase) falls; by all means, do not follow along with dullness or sinking, nor allow even the slightest external object to be grasped.
The single phrase of mindfulness of the Buddha—“Amitābha Buddha”—is the primary koan of the Zen school. It is like riding a horse while holding a staff;

it is a segment of one’s life that provides stability. Regardless of whether one belongs to the four classes of practitioners, if one maintains this practice, there will invariably be a response and verification, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.

Among these, do not let even a single recitation of Amitābha be interrupted. You must believe that because the cause is profound, the fruit is profound; you must ensure that even when you are not intentionally reciting, it recites itself.

If you can maintain this mindfulness without a single thought being empty, it will surely coalesce into a single mass. When, in the midst of recitation, you recognize the one who is reciting, Amitābha and I will appear together.
Thus, you shall enter the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, personally realize the Inner Court of Sukhāvatī, and reach the destination of the Lotus Womb.

As for one’s name, those who have attained ultimate merit will see it for themselves; they shall personally witness Amitābha bestowing upon them a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), at which point they become companions to the Bodhisattvas.
From this moment on, they depart from the Sahā world, traveling a path entirely free of sorrow or affliction until reaching unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Thereafter, for eternal kalpas, they may roam freely according to their hearts’ desire. Having returned by relying upon this Way, they are certain to achieve Buddhahood without deficiency.
To reveal what constitutes true inquiry and genuine awakening: it does not consist in attaining a single phrase through mental cultivation until it becomes familiar;
nor does it arise naturally over time from maintaining ten thousand dharmas or the "Mu" koan; nor does it lie in the hardship of sitting for long periods without lying down.
This is caused by the demon of sleep. Why? Because it is summoned when a person lacks right mindfulness and right energy. Generally, one must possess the power of the wisdom of observation;
at every moment, one must doubt oneself and attack one's own delusions. Only after such self-attack and transformation have continued for a long time will worldly afflictions be stilled.
The pure body manifests before you; suddenly, according to your capacity, it is stirred into awakening to your original nature.

Your entire being is the Buddha. Do not allow yourself to further differentiate between mind and nature; you will naturally attain a field of peace and bliss. If even a single dharma is not clearly understood, [you have not attained it].
One uses it to clarify what is not yet understood; one uses it to penetrate what is not yet realized.

There is no evil that is not eliminated, no goodness that is not cultivated, no merit that is not perfected, and no principle that is not clarified—only then is the Path of the Sages accomplished. Even after one has awakened to and clearly realized the fundamental essence...

One should simply rest there. Those who cannot penetrate the gateways of transformation and the cultural refinements of the teachings are what the ancients called "stuck atop a hundred-foot pole" or "fallen into the minor fruits of the Two Vehicles"; they will ultimately never reach the ocean of all-knowledge.

Therefore, the Great Awakened One said: "Letting go at the edge of a precipice, one spontaneously accepts the responsibility; after death and returning to life, one cannot deceive the Master. How could this be empty talk?
Ah! Furthermore, I have not yet discerned from where the application of effort begins, where it reaches its halfway point, and where it reaches completion. There is this analogy for this.
“I shall believe you only when you speak thus. Huáng’s elder brother said, “It is exactly as you have asked; only then may I explain it to you.

In general, every person possesses the Buddha-nature. It is simply because one lacks the Buddha-wisdom to shatter the afflictions that the conditions for their union cannot be met, and one remains bound by present emotional defilements.
It is like the making of wine in the world: although it contains [the ingredients],”
Rice and water. The flour provides the great power; yet if there is no power of the *qu* (fermenting agent) to attack and transform it, wine will ultimately not be produced.
A person’s Buddha-nature is likened to the rice, and the conditions for merit are likened to the water.

Thus, although one possesses the nature, the merit, and the conditions, if there is no great wisdom and great insight to inwardly attack and inwardly transform it, one will ultimately not become a Buddha, but will merely be called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). This is especially true for those who apply themselves to spiritual practice.

Diligently set aside all that you have done throughout your life, whether right or wrong. Hold fast to a single phrase of the primary koan (*benzan watō*), questioning it yourself and doubting yourself;
question and doubt yourself, pressuring and pursuing yourself, attacking and investigating yourself.

Do not permit others to explain it for you, nor permit yourself to clarify it through intellectual interpretation. You must strive to master the phrase thoroughly and suddenly sever the root of your life.

In this manner, pressed on day and night three times each, as the years passed and months deepened, suddenly one day, without deliberate thought, there naturally flow from the mouth one or two lines, or four or eight lines of words that accord with the occasion and meet the standard.
This is called the realm of intelligence (*caitanya-viṣaya*). Generally speaking, those who have awakened to the Way all pass through this realm of intelligence; yet one must not [rest there].
Acknowledge it. Relying on what was previously pressed upon you, suddenly one day words of hundreds of thousands of verses will flow forth from the mouth as if one’s entire body were a mouth.
Do not let go at all; this is precisely when you must apply effort and exert yourself. It is like the brewing of wine: after the great boiling, one must pour it out and let it settle before it stops.
When a person applies their work until they pass through the state of mere cleverness, great awakening will manifest before them. This happens frequently.
He has thoroughly investigated and fully resolved every one of the seventeen hundred ancient koans,
until there is no Zen left to study, no Buddha to cultivate, and no Dharma to doubt, such that he has attained realization in every single instance.
Every single thing penetrates upward; whatever comes forth from the mouth of faith accords with the ancient standard. At that time, one understands by oneself and does not understand through another;

one rests by oneself and does not rest through another. Without waiting for anything to be set aside, one naturally comes to rest, like a person who has arrived home and no longer worries about the path.
Only then is one called a person whose practice has reached its consummation.
Xingshi was a man of Xian in Min. His father’s surname was Cai and his mother’s Huang. He left home at the age of twenty-seven;
the rest is not recorded. Zuhong said: "The verses for exhorting mindfulness of the Buddha are excellent; I have edited them to remove redundant phrases."

Master Xixian Bao ascended the hall and raised the case of the World-Honored One ascending the seat and Mañjuśrī striking the mallet. The Master then said: "I do not recall when the Old Man with the Yellow Face..."
At such a time, one surely knows there is this very moment. Yet, alas, it remains that one has not yet met a true connoisseur. Often, those of the scholastic schools say:
"When the World-Honored One ascended the seat and Mañjuśrī struck the gavel, this was indeed a meeting of masters, a harmonious exchange between teacher and disciple.

This is because they do not realize that Mañjuśrī, with his many-tongued mouth, was merely following the lead at the assembly and framing a false accusation; they have let him off far too easily. Today, this mountain monk...
He neither imitated their conduct nor acted alone; his noble desire was to find a fellow traveler who could come forth and join him arm-in-arm.
How could this not be considered a fine deed? He then took up his staff and said, "Is there anyone? Is there anyone? At that moment, a monk came forward and prostrated.
[The Master] struck him across the back and said, "Why so talkative? The monk said, "I have said but a single word."
"It has not yet been brought forth. Why such talkativeness? The Master struck him again and said, "A second offense will not be tolerated.
On the following day, he ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday I raised the koan of the World-Honored One ascending the seat; the case was not yet resolved.
I have not been able to unravel the delusions of you all, nor have I been able to cause you all to walk hand-in-hand with the World-Honored One. Why is this? If you are one who knows the sound."
The author: As soon as one acts thus, one immediately understands not to act thus; thereafter, there is no further connection.
One must simply let go of both extremes and cast down the middle. Then, naturally vivid and alert, one becomes the master wherever one is.

Like water poured into water, like space merging with space—neither Buddhas nor patriarchs can know it, and neither ghosts nor gods can fathom it. Even if one reaches this state, if one wishes to interact with the world...

The Venerable One’s wrists were clasped together, yet there remained a single thread-like gap between them. If one wishes to open up and pass through this single thread, one must further listen as this mountain monk recites another verse:
“The Buddha’s body is equal to space, and the seat accords with the body; When has he ever ascended? When has he ever descended?
Mañjuśrī beheld a reflection and gave rise to the vision of wild flowers; Thus leading his descendants into a legacy of idle talk. He descended from the seat.
Regarding the "Nian Gu" (Citing the Ancient): Fuguo Qin, Fojian Jiqin, and Foyan Yuan were all serving the Fifth Patriarch late one night.
The Patriarch said, "Each of you provide a turning phrase. Fojian said, "A variegated phoenix dances in the crimson sky. Foyan said, "An iron snake lies across the ancient road."
Regarding this, Foguo said: "Look under your feet. The Patriarch [Fayan] said: "The one who will extinguish my school is Keqin.
Examining the words of these three men, is there a distinction of superiority or inferiority among them? If you say there is no distinction, why did the Fifth Patriarch speak in such a manner?
If one speaks of superiority and inferiority, where is the locus of such superiority and inferiority?
It is revealed that the Buddhas and sentient beings are but this single mind, with no other dharma apart from it. For the awakened, the mind is able to transform objects; as for objects—
All phenomena return to one's own mind; this is precisely the Buddhas. Those who are deluded turn their backs on the mind and face toward objects, falsely following after them as they shift;
these are sentient beings. Therefore, Buddhas and sentient beings are nothing other than this single mind; there is no separate dharma whatsoever.

Furthermore, when I, Śākyamuni Buddha, had not yet attained perfect enlightenment, I practiced asceticism for six years in the Snowy Mountains, reaching the ultimate limit of meditative concentration.
At midnight, he raised his head and saw the morning star appear; he attained a sudden, great enlightenment. What did he realize at that time? He realized "awakening" (*xing*).
It is simply awakening to one's own inherently existing mind, which is not obtained from others.

It is primordially manifest and primordially ever-present. Immediately thereafter, he universally observed all sentient beings throughout the great earth, seeing that each and every one of them possessed it.
The Tathāgata’s eternally abiding true mind is the seed-nature for attaining Buddhahood; yet, because of delusive thoughts and attachments, it cannot be realized.
Consequently, out of compassion, he universally delivers all beings through the teachings spoken over forty-nine years, none of which are ultimate truths.
All were done out of necessity, as he saw that sentient beings have much doubt and little faith, and are unable to achieve great, direct conviction.
From one’s own mind, myriad differences arise; thus, one cannot avoid administering medicine according to the illness, leading all provisional means back to the single reality.

Furthermore, fearing that all sentient beings might generate understanding based on words alone—clinging to verbal expressions and falling into the net of doctrine—he subsequently ascended the seat and did not utter a single word.
He merely held up a single branch of a blue lotus and gazed silently at the fourfold assembly, desiring for each person...
At that moment, one directly clarifies the original mind and personally encounters it face-to-face. Yet, unexpectedly, the great assembly still misses the mark.
Only Kāśyapa moved his countenance and smiled, thereby harmonizing with the fundamental capacity; thus, the Dharma was entrusted to him and he was established as the First Patriarch.
This transmission was passed down in succession until it reached the twenty-eighth patriarch, Venerable Bodhidharma, who observed that the sentient beings of this land possessed...
Possessing the capacity for the Mahāyāna, he then traveled west by sea. He pointed directly to the human mind so that one might see one's nature and attain Buddhahood;
he did not establish written texts nor rely on clever artifice. Only through this direct mind does one immediately realize it within oneself.

O Great Assembly, this very thing is what all Buddhas and Patriarchs since time immemorial have used to lead all sentient beings to directly awaken to the One Mind, see their nature, and attain Buddhahood.
This is the original draft. Master Xingshi said:
"I am of a prominent family from Jintai. My father was from Wumen and my mother was of the Ding clan. I entered the monastic life at the age of twenty and paid homage to Master Da..."

He took Master Jinen as his teacher. Thereafter, he traveled extensively to visit various spiritual friends (*kishi*). The circumstances of his cultivation, progress, awakening, and practice of the Way are fully recorded in his collected works;
fearing prolixity, they are not transcribed here.
Zhu Hong said: "I traveled to the capital and studied under both the masters Bianrong and Xiaoyan. In the following year, both masters passed away.

Master Rong possessed a single-minded sincerity and practiced accordingly; he left no writings to be transmitted to the world. Master Yan lived in obscurity within the willow lanes and seldom received visitors.
There exists a four-fascicle *Xiaoyan ji* (Anthology of Xiaoyan); here, I have excerpted a small portion of it."

I have appended here the epitaphs for various masters found within the collected works of the Song Dynasty scholar Xue Lian (Song Jinglao). Zhu Hong has excerpted a small portion of them to record the great achievements of the Sagely Court,
so that they shall not be lost to oblivion.
The Chan Master Guding Ming:
His name was Ming. He was the fifteenth-generation descendant of Linji. Having occupied four monastic seats, as he was about to pass away, he said to his disciples:

Avalokiteśvara appeared holding a lotus flower and arrived. He sat peacefully and passed away. Upon cremation, his tongue, teeth, jaw, and rosary remained unburnt, and countless śarīra relics of five colors were produced.
Mr. Wei composed an inscription for him in the National History. His *Recorded Sayings from Four Assemblies* is circulated in the world.
Chan Master Xuechuang Guang: His name was Wuguang;
his courtesy name was Gongsu; his surname was Yang; his style was Xuechuang. He was a native of Xindu in Chengdu.
By means of the power of samādhi, he entered the ocean of wisdom. Initially, he preached the Dharma at Baima Temple, and subsequently resided at Yuyang Tianwang Monastery.
Tong delivered sermons on four occasions. Duke Yu Wenqing praised him, stating that he was like a phoenix feather or a unicorn horn within the lineage of Fuguo.
This was recorded in the fourteenth year of the Hongwu era.
Chan Master Nantang Yu:
His name was Qingyu, his style name was Liaohan, and Nantang was his dharma title. He belonged to the Zhu clan and was a native of Linhai in Taizhou.
He resided at the three monasteries of Kaifu, Benjue, and Lingyan, for which there exist three records of his formal discourses (*yulu*).
Master Yuekong of Mount Jing, whose secular name was Yan Gong,
being the legitimate successor of Dongyu, resided at Dong Chan in Kunshan, then moved to Wanshou in Wumen, and subsequently ascended [to higher positions].
From Hulin and Nanping, he proceeded to ascend the Double Path (Shuangjing).

There exists the *Siyi Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of the Four Assemblies), in which his late teacher, the Duke Wenxian Wang, appearing in the body of a secular official, propagated the Prajñāpāramitā and maintained a relationship of "external friendship" with the Chan Master.
Songyue Yin Gong praised the Master’s Way as being superior even to those of Yuanzhao and Fozhao.
Zhu Hong said: "The recorded sayings (*yulu*) from the four assemblies no longer exist, and I do not even know where Songyue is now.
Yet [you] claim his realization was superior to that of Yuanzhao and Fozhao. Surely those two masters were not easily equaled;
to say he surpassed them requires further examination and correction by a worthy scholar."

When Chan Master Foguang was young, he would sit in meditation during the middle of the night. Whenever his mother pushed him over, he would immediately sit up again and remain awake until dawn. Later, he left the household life and studied under Master Quan of Yunju.
Day and night, he focused his mindfulness. One evening, beneath the moonlight on the pines, he attained realization upon hearing the sound of flowing water. He then went...
He visited Master Baiquan. Master Quan sent him to visit Gulin. Gulin asked, "You clearly know that the four elements and five aggregates are the root of birth and death;
why have you entered this leather bag? As the Master hesitated, Gulin struck him with his staff, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment.
He resided at Qingliang for fifteen years and later retired to Dongtang, never venturing beyond the mountains. He lived to the age of eighty.

5. At seventy years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*), he passed away. Seven days later, his countenance remained bright and lustrous, and the crown of his head was still warm. His *śarīra* were like pearls and jade, it is said.
Master Jin of Bifeng.

The Master’s name was Baokim; his surname was Shi, and his style name was Bifeng. He was born in Yongshou County of Hangzhou. At the age of six, he left the household life and traveled extensively to study under various lecture masters.
He attended upon the master Zhen Gongruhe, to the point that he neglected both sleep and food. While following the master to gather wild vegetables, he suddenly sat in meditation, motionless.

Later, he entered a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and did not arise for many days. Once, while sitting beneath a tree, a mountain stream surged across the path; people thought the Master had been swept away.
He drowned. After seven days had passed, he sat upright as if in his normal state. One day, hearing the sound of wood being felled, sweat poured from him like rain.

He sought verification from the Master (the Emperor), who confirmed it with his seal of approval. In the second year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to the capital and received the utmost imperial favors.
When the Master fell ill, the Sovereign personally inscribed his calligraphy and bestowed upon him a twelve-line poem. On the fourth day of the sixth month, he bathed and changed his robes.
He passed away sitting upright with his robes adjusted. His worldly age was sixty-five, and his years as a monk were fifty. He was cremated;
five-colored śarīras emerged in profusion, while his teeth, tongue, and prayer beads remained unaltered.
Chan Master Dongming: His name was Huirì;

his style name was Dongming. He was a native of Chìchéng on Mount Tiantái. At the beginning of the Hongwǔ era, he was summoned to the capital, where his responses to the Emperor’s inquiries met with the Sovereign’s approval.
Later, he took leave to return to Tiānzhú in Hángzhōu, where he cultivated the pure practices of the Western Paradise. This was in the twelfth year of the Hongwǔ era.
On the first day of the seventh month, he said to his disciples: "In my dream, I saw a pond of blue lotuses whose pure fragrance overwhelmed me.
It seems I am about to depart. On the fourth day, he passed away while seated. His worldly age was eighty-nine, and his years of monastic seniority were seventy.
Toward kings, dukes, and high ministers, the Master never uttered a single word of flattery; yet in encouraging and guiding later students, he was as warm and gentle as spring.
Yang said:
Chan Master Gufeng De’s name was Mingde;
his style name was Gufeng. He became a monk at the age of fifteen and went to visit Master Zhuxi Tan. The Master asked him, "Where have you come from?"
He said, "A golden goose has arrived. He asked again, "How high is Mount Jinge? The Master replied, "One cannot see its peak. Zhuxi rebuked him.
One day, he raised the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower. Upon hearing this, the Master suddenly attained realization.
He then went to visit Huiji Xigong of Jingci Temple. Xigong asked, "Who is it that comes in such a manner? The Master replied, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi."
Fourth: He also visited Master Mingji Jun at Shuanglin and Master Zhutian Lin; his many doubts were resolved like ice melting away.

On the twenty-seventh day of the second month in the fifth year of the Hongwu era, he passed away while seated. His secular age was seventy-nine, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was sixty-two.
After his body was cremated, his cranial bone remained indestructible, and śarīra relics emerged in profusion from the ashes. Four volumes of his recorded sayings (*yǔlù*) circulate in the world.

The characters have a small basis for their origin; do not move them at all, and do not alter or add to them.
Simply, throughout the twelve periods of the day and within the four modes of deportment, raise up the *huatou*. Do not wait to see whether or not you will attain enlightenment at some point;

do not concern yourself with whether there is flavor or no flavor, nor with whether you gain power or not. Press on until the mind can no longer reach it and the intellect can no longer conceive of it.
"Practice. This is precisely where all Buddhas and patriarchs relinquished their bodies and lives.
